title: K Closest Points to Origin
description: Brute force to optimized: fully sorting every point by distance versus a max-heap capped at size k, keeping only the current closest candidates.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of points on the X-Y plane and an integer k, return the k points closest to the origin (0, 0), in any order.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Among all the given points, find the k whose distance to the origin is smallest, returning them in any order.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the k Nearest Shops to Home on a Map
blocks.text: Picture a map with many shop locations, and needing to find just the k closest ones to home, without needing to know the exact distance-sorted order of every single shop on the map.

blocks.caption: A max-heap capped at size k always holds the current k closest points

blocks.text: (-2,2) is closer to the origin than (1,3), so the closest 1 point is [[-2,2]].
The 2 closest points are [[3,3],[-2,4]] (order may vary).
Before fully sorting every point by its distance, notice that only the k smallest distances are ever needed, exactly what a size-capped max-heap tracks directly.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The squared distance, x squared plus y squared, preserves the same relative ordering as true distance, avoiding unnecessary square root computations.

Observation 2: A max-heap capped at size k, ordered by distance, always holds the current k CLOSEST points, with the FARTHEST of those k sitting at the top.

Observation 3: For each new point, if the heap has fewer than k points, add it directly; otherwise, compare it to the current worst of the top k (the heap's top) and swap it in only if it is closer.

Observation 4: After processing every point, the heap holds exactly the k closest points.
This leads to maintaining a max-heap of size k (ordered by distance), pushing each point in and popping the farthest whenever the heap exceeds size k.
Sort every point by its distance to the origin, and take the first k.

items: Compute the squared distance to the origin for every point.
Sort all points by this distance.
Return the first k points from the sorted list.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every point is fully sorted by distance, even though only the k smallest distances are ever needed.
The first k entries of the sorted list are simply sliced off at the end.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), sorting every point.
Space: O(n) for the sorted copy.
Limitation: fully sorting every point is unnecessary work when only the k closest are ever needed, a size-capped heap avoids sorting anything beyond those k.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why full sorting is unnecessary: only the k smallest distances matter, not the exact order of every point beyond them.

What tracks the current best k efficiently: a max-heap capped at size k, ordered by distance, whose top is always the farthest among the current best k.

How new points are processed: push each point in; if the heap exceeds size k, pop the farthest, since it is no longer among the k closest.

The core idea: maintain a size-k max-heap by distance; after processing every point, the heap holds exactly the k closest.

Maintain a max-heap ordered by squared distance, capped at size k. For each point, push it onto the heap; if the heap now holds more than k points, pop the one with the largest distance. After processing every point, the heap contains exactly the k closest points.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: size-k max-heap by distance, pop the farthest when it overflows

blocks.text: A max-heap capped at size k always holds the current k smallest-distance points seen so far, since any point that would make the heap exceed size k is only removed if it is the FARTHEST among the current top k plus the new point, guaranteeing every point that stays is genuinely among the k closest seen at that point. After every point has been processed, exactly the k closest overall remain.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log k), each of n points triggering at most one O(log k) heap operation.
Space: O(k) for the heap.

blocks.text: K Closest Points to Origin is a direct application of the size-capped heap pattern: whenever only the top (or bottom) k elements of a collection are needed, a heap of size k avoids the cost of fully sorting everything.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid sorting everything", think: a max-heap capped at size k keeps only the current best k candidates.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n log n) time and O(n) space. The optimized size-k max-heap runs in O(n log k) time and O(k) space.

items: Pattern: a max-heap capped at size k, keeping only the current best k candidates.
Core Idea: push each point's squared distance onto a size-k max-heap, popping the farthest whenever it overflows; the heap ends up holding exactly the k closest points.
Time: O(n log n) for the brute force, O(n log k) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n) for the brute force, O(k) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: only the k smallest distances are ever needed, making a full sort unnecessary.
Interview Difficulty: a standard, well-known heap application.
One line memory trick: size-k max-heap by distance; pop the farthest on overflow.
